hints: Look closely at what changes, you start with one Br on a saturated alkane and end with two Br atoms on adjacent carbons.
First you need to remove HBr from 1-bromopropane to make the alkene propene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$.
Now think what happens when that C=C double bond reacts with bromine, $\text{Br}_2$, and which reaction type adds two atoms across the double bond.
walkthrough:
**Compare start and finish**

Great first habit, always draw or picture the carbon skeletons. You start with $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ and want $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{Br}$.

You cannot go directly from one Br to two Br by substitution. You need an alkene in the middle.

**Step 1 - Make the alkene by elimination**

A bromoalkane loses HBr when heated with ethanolic NaOH. This is dehydrohalogenation, a type of elimination.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2 + \text{HBr}$$

**Step 2 - Add bromine by addition**

Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition with bromine at room temperature. The $\text{Br-Br}$ adds across the C=C to give adjacent dibromo groups.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{Br}$$

So the sequence is elimination then addition.

options.A: Incorrect. Addition cannot be step 1 because 1-bromopropane is saturated and has no C=C to add to. Substitution as step 2 would only swap one group for one Br, not add two Br atoms.
options.B: Correct. Step 1 elimination with ethanolic NaOH gives propene, step 2 electrophilic addition of $\text{Br}_2$ to propene gives 1,2-dibromopropane. This is the classic haloalkane to alkene to dihaloalkane route.
options.C: Incorrect. Hydrolysis (aqueous NaOH) of 1-bromopropane would give propan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, which does not help you get to a dibromide. Elimination from an alcohol needs concentrated acid and still would not give the second Br.
options.D: Incorrect. Substitution then hydrolysis both give single functional group products, for example an alcohol or nitrile then an alcohol. Neither step creates a C=C bond or adds two bromine atoms across adjacent carbons.
